title: Judaism: study is holy
hookLine: learning is itself worship, and argument is honored (Pirkei Avot 1.1)

lines: THE SOUND OF SOMETHING GOING RIGHT.
cards: A room full of long tables. Two people sit across from each other with one big book open between them, and they are arguing. Not whispering.

Arguing, out loud, fingers on the page, one shaking her head, the other laughing. Pair after pair like that, all at once, loud as a train station. To a stranger it might sound like something has gone wrong.
In a traditional Jewish house of study, it's the sound of something going right. Today: why study itself can be holy, and why the arguing is part of it.

teach.b: Start with the word. Torah. In the narrowest sense it means the five books of Moses, the scroll in the ark of a synagogue.

The Hebrew root has to do with teaching, pointing the way, so the word also stretches to mean all Jewish teaching, the whole conversation that grew around the scroll. That conversation has a well-known first line.

teach.h: A CHAIN FROM SINAI, HAND TO HAND.
teach.b: Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, a short book of sayings in the Mishnah, opens by tracing a chain: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and on to the teachers of the great assembly.
Learning is handed from person to person, like a lamp passed down a line. The Torah itself asks for this.

Right after the Shema, Deuteronomy says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children." Teaching the young isn't a hobby here; it sits inside the central prayer.
Then the surprise: Jewish tradition honors argument. The Talmud records the debates of two ancient schools, the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, who disagreed again and again.

teach.h: BOTH ARE WORDS OF THE LIVING GOD.
teach.b: A heavenly voice, the story goes, declared that both were the words of the living God, and the law followed Hillel partly because his students were humble and taught Shammai's view before their own.
And study often happens in pairs, called chavruta, from the word for friend.
You don't learn alone. You push, your partner pushes back, and the text opens.

how: Many Jews study Torah and Talmud in pairs called chavruta, reading aloud and debating line by line, and a weekly portion of the Torah is read in synagogue through the year.

games.q: two schools disagree again and again. a voice from heaven speaks. what does it say?
o: both are the words of the living God.
games.why: the Talmud says both were the words of the living God, and the law followed Hillel, whose students taught the other side first.

practice: Take one line, any you've met on this path, or today's, teach them diligently, and say it once, slowly. Now imagine a partner across from you, asking who them is, and what diligently looks like on a Tuesday.
Let the question sit; you don't need an answer yet.

wordCard.voice: Torah. From a root about teaching and pointing the way: the five books of Moses, and the whole living conversation around them. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: teaching, instruction; many Ashkenazi Jews say TOY-rah.

carryVoice: Your line: learn together. A lamp passed hand to hand, and argued over on the way. That's day two hundred forty-eight.
